input.reasoning:
Searched thirteen framings: the claim as written and as proposed, short paraphrases, three negations ("saturons do not exhibit suppressed decay", "decay is not suppressed at half capacity"), vocabulary variants (maximum entropy within a region, objects saturating information bounds), and effect-naming variants. Only one existing claim ever surfaced: the black-hole-specific memory burden claim, under four different framings, topping out at 0.678 similarity. Nothing in the graph states the general saturon proposition in either polarity.

The near-miss is a generalization relationship, not identity. The existing claim is about black hole evaporation specifically and would be assessed through black-hole-specific considerations (Hawking evaporation, the Page time, evaporation histories). The proposed claim is about saturons as a class and turns on considerations that do not reduce to the black hole case: whether generic information-saturating systems (solitons, monopoles, analogue systems, bound states) exhibit the same suppression. Evidence can come apart in both directions: a laboratory analogue showing suppressed decay bears directly on the general claim and only indirectly on black hole evaporation, and black-hole-specific semiclassical results bear on the instance without settling the class. Under the identical-decomposition test of §2 they are different claims, so I created the new node rather than forcing the general proposition into the black-hole-specific page, which would have split the class-level debate across the wrong home. Per the recoverable-error preference, if the Curator later judges them one claim, a merge is cheap; this direction is not.

On wording: I adjusted the proposed form to name the effect the discourse actually names. The proposition under debate is commonly posed as "the memory burden effect is generic to saturons", and naming the thesis follows the canonical-direction rule; it also keeps the family coherent with the black-hole-specific claim, which already uses the effect's name. The proposition, the half-loss threshold, and the class are unchanged from the proposed form.
input.direction_note: Stated as the affirmative form of the live question in the memory-burden literature, whether decay suppression after roughly half of the information is lost is a generic property of saturons rather than specific to black holes; the effect and the class are named as the discourse names them.
input.new_canonical_form: The memory burden effect suppresses the decay of any saturon once roughly half of its information is lost
input.relationship_notes: The memory burden black hole claim (351acde4-828d-43f8-a6a9-eb33d64391e4) is the closest relative and the reason this search was non-trivial: the new claim is its generalization, and the black hole case is its flagship instance, contingent on black holes being saturons. Evidence on the generic claim bears on the black hole claim through that instance premise, but their assessments should be held separately since the considerations differ. The Planck-scale remnant claim (06c90251-420a-48a3-8724-4c110c7c8094) is a rival mechanism for late-time evaporation cessation and constrains this claim: if evaporation halts for Planck-scale reasons, the memory burden explanation loses support. The microscopic black hole claim (960a19bf-e34a-4606-bb98-96aca57fb4bc) that they evaporate essentially instantly is in tension with any claim that decay is suppressed partway, and both cannot comfortably hold at high credence together.
